strengths: Addresses a timely and underexplored problem: mitigating the security degradation caused by purely benign instruction fine-tuning (as opposed to the more commonly studied scenario of malicious data mixed into training).

Presents a coherent pipeline: builds a lightweight security-feature proxy classifier, uses it to probe module-level robustness via systematic parameter perturbations, distills the findings into three consistent patterns (shallow-layer sensitivity, Q/K sensitivity, collaborative effects across modules), and translates these into a concrete, cheap-to-implement mitigation (differentiated learning rates).

Fairly extensive empirical evaluation across five open-source LLMs (Llama2-7B/13B, Llama3.1-8B, Vicuna-7B/13B), two training regimes (general-domain and a custom specific-domain math task), and seven attack types (two red-team sets, three automated jailbreaks, two manual jailbreaks), with consistent security gains reported.

Includes several sanity-check ablations that address plausible confounds, e.g., matching training loss/checkpoints between standard IFT and ML-LR to rule out under-fitting artifacts, and extending LoRA to all modules to test flexibility.

The proposed patterns (module robustness varying by depth and type) are independently corroborated by a follow-up experiment (Sec. 6.2) that trains only shallow/middle/deep layers and observes the expected security trend, lending some validity to the proxy-based analysis beyond the classifier alone.
Usability/expertise preservation is explicitly measured and shown to be largely unaffected, which is important for a method proposing to trade off some fine-tuning freedom for security.
weaknesses: No comparison against existing parameter/representation-based defenses for fine-tuning-induced safety degradation (e.g., Vaccine, Booster, RepNoise, or even simple baselines like a uniformly smaller global learning rate, layer freezing, or L2-regularization toward the base model). Without such baselines it is hard to know whether the proxy-guided module selection is meaningfully better than much simpler heuristics that would achieve a similar train-conservatively-in-early-layers effect.

The security proxy is a simple linear classifier trained on only 100 minimally-edited malicious/benign instruction pairs derived solely from AdvBench; its ability to generalize as a faithful stand-in for broader model 'security' (across topics, languages, or jailbreak strategies) is not independently validated, yet it underlies the entire module robustness analysis and search algorithm.

The perturbation methodology (zeroing half of rows/columns of a module's weight matrix) is a coarse and somewhat arbitrary probe; the causal link between this drastic ablation and the effect of gradient updates during actual fine-tuning is asserted rather than rigorously established.

Learning-rate hyperparameters differ by up to four orders of magnitude (e.g., 2e-4 vs 2e-8) and are set per scenario/model without a clear principled procedure for choosing them on unseen models, raising reproducibility and generalizability concerns for practitioners who would need to redo the full profiling/search pipeline for each new base model.

Security evaluation relies entirely on a single GPT-4-based automatic judge (GPT-Judge) with no human verification or inter-rater reliability check, and no multiple-seed or variance/statistical-significance reporting across the many experimental conditions.

The 'specific-domain' scenario uses an artificial, self-defined math operator task rather than a realistic domain (coding, medical, legal), which limits how strongly the results generalize to real-world specific-domain benign IFT use cases.

ML-LR requires 2-3 additional training epochs to match standard IFT's task performance, and the added computational/engineering overhead of building the proxy, running the perturbation sweep, and the search algorithm is not analyzed in terms of cost versus benefit relative to simpler alternatives.

Framing the work as a 'pioneering effort' somewhat overstates novelty given related work on safety-preserving fine-tuning parameter constraints, even though the specific benign-only setting is a valid distinguishing motivation.

strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important problem: security degradation from benign instruction fine-tuning, distinct from the more commonly studied 'malicious data mixed into training' setting.

Reasonably broad empirical scope: five open-source LLMs (Llama2-7B/13B, Llama3.1-8B, Vicuna-7B/13B), multiple attack families (red-team, automated jailbreaks GCG/PAIR/AutoDAN, manual jailbreaks SAP30/Comp_Obj), and two usage scenarios (general-domain and a specific-domain math task).

Includes several sanity-check analyses (extending LoRA to all modules, quantitative verification of Pattern A, addressing insufficient-training-loss confound), showing some awareness of potential confounds.

The overall pipeline (proxy classifier -> perturbation-based module analysis -> search algorithm -> differentiated learning rate) is clearly described with pseudocode and appendix detail, aiding reproducibility of the mechanics if not the underlying claims.
weaknesses: The central proxy—a linear classifier trained on only 200 minimally-edited instruction pairs—has not been validated as a faithful stand-in for actual downstream security (measured via GPT-Judge harmfulness on red-team/jailbreak attacks). The leap from 'perturbation changes proxy accuracy on a tiny curated set' to 'this identifies modules causally responsible for real-world jailbreak vulnerability' is asserted rather than demonstrated with independent validation.

The core ablation needed to justify the method's necessity is missing: is the benefit driven by correctly identifying 'robust' modules, or simply by applying a much smaller learning rate to a large fraction of modules generally (a 4-order-of-magnitude LR gap, 2e-4 vs 2e-8)? No comparison to naive baselines (e.g., random module subset with the same LR split, uniform small global LR, or freezing shallow layers only) is provided, so the paper cannot rule out that a much simpler intervention would achieve similar mitigation.

No other safety-preserving fine-tuning baselines from the literature (e.g., Vaccine, Booster, Lisa, or other layer/LR-based defenses cited in Related Work) are compared against, despite these being directly relevant alternatives; this limits the ability to judge the marginal contribution of the proposed search algorithm.

No statistical variance reporting (single training runs, no seeds/error bars) despite differences between IFT and ML-LR sometimes being modest (e.g., 0.2–0.5 HS points, single-digit ASR percentage points in several cells), leaving open whether reported gains are robust to run-to-run variance or judge noise.

Residual harmfulness after applying ML-LR remains substantial for several strong attacks (e.g., PAIR/AutoDAN scores frequently still 2.0–2.6), which somewhat undercuts the abstract's claim of 'significantly mitigating' the harmfulness rise; the method appears to be a partial mitigation rather than a resolution of the underlying problem.

The specific-domain evaluation relies on an artificial constructed task (novel arithmetic operator symbols) rather than a genuine specific-domain capability (e.g., code, math reasoning, medical QA) mentioned as motivation in the introduction, weakening the ecological validity of the 'real application' claim.

Checkpoint selection procedures differ between conditions (standard IFT vs. ML-LR use different numbers of epochs, chosen post hoc based on accuracy/loss), which, combined with the lack of a principled early-stopping criterion, introduces potential experimenter degrees of freedom that could bias comparisons.

Reliance on a specific GPT-4 preview endpoint (gpt-4-1106-preview) for the harmfulness judge raises reproducibility concerns, since the exact model behavior may not be recoverable as the API evolves or is deprecated.
The extra training cost (2-3 additional epochs) required to match expertise under ML-LR is acknowledged but not quantified or factored into the cost-benefit narrative of the proposed method.

strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important problem: security degradation from purely benign instruction fine-tuning, which is less studied than the malicious-data-mixing scenario.

The module-level robustness analysis is a novel and interesting angle, yielding clear, consistent patterns (shallow-vs-deep sensitivity, Q/K sensitivity, collaborative/non-additive effects across modules) that are corroborated across four different LLM families (Llama2-7B/13B, Llama3.1-8B, Vicuna-7B/13B).

The proposed ML-LR strategy is simple, lightweight (no extra parameters, only differentiated learning rates), and is evaluated fairly broadly: two realistic scenarios (general-domain simulation and a specific-domain math task), multiple red-team and jailbreak attack methods, and both security and usability/expertise metrics.

Several targeted ablations strengthen the internal validity of the claims, e.g., verifying Pattern A via direct layer-wise training, testing the strategy when LoRA is extended to all modules, and addressing the potential confound of insufficient training-data fitting via a controlled checkpoint/loss comparison.
Detailed appendix with full quantitative results, pseudocode for the search algorithm, and evaluation examples supports partial reproducibility.
weaknesses: The security proxy classifier that underlies the entire module analysis is trained on only 100 instruction pairs derived from a single template-editing procedure (minimal word substitution from AdvBench); this is a narrow, small, and potentially unrepresentative basis for identifying generalizable 'security-related modules,' and its high held-out accuracy on only 100 similarly-constructed test pairs does not strongly establish that it captures a general notion of LLM security.

The causal link between the perturbation-based proxy sensitivity (zeroing rows/columns of weight matrices) and actual security degradation from gradient-based fine-tuning is assumed rather than tightly established; the zero-perturbation operation is a crude and somewhat arbitrary probe that may not reflect how fine-tuning gradients actually alter these modules.

No comparison to existing parameter-based or representation-based defenses against fine-tuning-induced harm (e.g., Vaccine, Booster, RepNoise, mentioned in related work) is provided, even as baselines, making it hard to judge the relative merit of ML-LR against the existing toolbox of mitigation techniques.

Checkpoint selection across experiments appears somewhat ad hoc and asymmetric between standard IFT and ML-LR (e.g., choosing checkpoints with 'accuracy close to the best,' or comparing different epoch counts), which, despite the authors' attempt to address it via a loss-matched control experiment, leaves some risk of selection bias favoring the proposed method.

All harmfulness and usability judgments rely solely on GPT-4-based automatic judges (GPT-Judge, Just-Eval) without any human validation or inter-rater reliability check, and results appear to be single-run (no variance/repeated-trial reporting), limiting confidence in the precision of the reported point differences.

The specific-domain evaluation uses a custom, narrow synthetic task (novel arithmetic operator symbols) rather than a realistic specialized domain (e.g., code, medical, legal), which limits how well the 'real-world applicability' claim is supported.

The method still leaves nontrivial residual security degradation after fine-tuning (harmfulness/ASR reduced but not restored to base-model levels) and requires 2-3x more training epochs to match baseline expertise, a practical cost that is not clearly foregrounded as a limitation.

The search algorithm's hyperparameters/patterns (e.g., which layers/modules are 'robust') must be re-derived per architecture via the same proxy-and-perturbation pipeline, raising questions about scalability and transferability to new or larger models without repeating the full analysis.

strengths: Addresses an underexplored angle (in-training defenses) in the IFT security literature, motivated by the documented failure of a prior in-training baseline (Wei et al., 2024b), giving the work a clear positioning and gap to fill.

The classifier-based probing methodology for security feature space drift and the module-level robustness analysis (Patterns A, B, C) provide an interesting, relatively original diagnostic lens that motivates the proposed method rather than presenting SWAT as an ad hoc heuristic.

Extensive empirical evaluation across three LLMs (Llama2-7B, Llama3-8B, Qwen2-7B), two IFT datasets, benign and attack-data scenarios, multiple red-team and jailbreak benchmarks, and several strong pre-/post-training baselines (LoRAsafe, IFTsafe, Resta, Restad), with consistent ASR/HS improvements.
Demonstrated compatibility with existing pre-/post-training defenses, generally yielding compounding security gains, which is practically useful.

Includes supporting mechanistic analyses (performance of Mwarm, parameter update magnitude comparisons, independent verification of Pattern A) that go beyond headline numbers to substantiate the proposed mechanism.
Reasonable reproducibility support: LoRA hyperparameters, training epochs, evaluation protocols, and the ModsRob search algorithm are specified in the main text and appendix.
weaknesses: Figures 7 and 8 (Appendix E, verification of Pattern A for Llama3-8B and Qwen2-7B) report identical HS values to Figure 6 (Llama2-7B): [0,4] HS 2.55/3.79/3.44 and [28,32] HS 1.43/1.39/1.54 appear duplicated verbatim across three supposedly different models, which raises concerns about copy-paste errors or unreported/incorrect results and undermines confidence in the rigor of the verification experiments.

The ModsRob search (Algorithm 1) relies on several arbitrary design choices (e.g., a fixed 0.5% accuracy-drop threshold, restricting search to the latter half of layers, greedy depth/breadth heuristics) without ablation or sensitivity analysis, making it unclear how robust the identified module subset and resulting gains are to these choices.

All experiments use LoRA fine-tuning only; the original security-risk phenomenon (Qi et al., 2023) and much of the threat model literature concern full fine-tuning as well, so the generalizability of SWAT to full-parameter IFT is untested.

Task-performance evaluation is limited to math/reasoning benchmarks (UltraInteract, GSM8K) despite the introduction motivating IFT risks across coding, medical, and other domains; the paper does not show the method generalizes beyond this narrow setting.

Some combined-method results are inconsistent or catastrophic (e.g., Table 5 'w Both' completely destroys Llama3-8B's language ability; Table 6 'w Both' for Qwen2-7B shows a negative ∆ASR relative to baseline) but these failure cases are not discussed, analyzed, or explained in the text.

The security feature space drift analysis relies on a small, manually curated classifier training/test set (100/100 pairs derived from AdvBench paraphrases), which may limit the generality and statistical robustness of the drift and robustness-pattern claims.

No variance/repeated-run statistics are reported for the main results, so it is unclear whether reported ASR/HS differences (some quite small, e.g., 0.4 HS) are robust to random seed or training variation.

Writing contains minor but noticeable lapses (e.g., 'Securty-oriented', awkward phrasing in the abstract/intro, inconsistent capitalization of 'PATTERN') suggesting the manuscript would benefit from more careful proofreading.

strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important problem: security degradation of LLMs caused by instruction fine-tuning, with a largely unexplored in-training mitigation angle (as opposed to the more commonly studied pre-/post-training interventions).

The experimental protocol is reasonably broad: three base models (Llama2-7B, Llama3-8B, Qwen2-7B), two IFT datasets (UltraInteract, GSM8K), benign and attack-data scenarios, several red-team and jailbreak benchmarks, and comparison against multiple strong baselines (LoRA-safe, Resta/Resta_d, IFT-safe), including combinations with SWAT.

The method is motivated by an interpretability-style analysis (probing classifiers on hidden representations, module-level perturbation) rather than being purely ad hoc, and the paper includes follow-up analyses (parameter update magnitude, loss trajectory of M_warm, verification of Pattern A) that attempt to substantiate the proposed mechanism.
Reports consistent improvements in ASR/HS over standard IFT and baselines while largely preserving task accuracy, and shows that SWAT composes with pre-/post-training defenses for further gains.
weaknesses: The central empirical support for 'security feature space drift' rests on a single linear probe trained on only 100 hand-crafted benign/malicious instruction pairs (100 held out for testing); differences of a few percentage points (e.g., 95% vs 99%) are used to draw strong causal-sounding conclusions without any variance/significance analysis, multiple seeds, or larger/more diverse probing data.

The module-level 'robustness' analysis relies on a crude perturbation heuristic (zeroing half the rows/columns of Q/K/V/O weight matrices) as a proxy for how modules will behave during actual gradient-based fine-tuning; the link between this static pruning-based robustness signal and training dynamics is asserted rather than rigorously justified.

The ModsRob search algorithm (Alg. 1) is a greedy, heuristic procedure with an arbitrary threshold (acc_base − 0.5%), and no ablation demonstrates that this specific search strategy is necessary/optimal versus simpler alternatives (e.g., fixed last-N-layers warm-up).

Several results undermine the claimed robustness of the method: Table 5 shows that combining SWAT with both IFT-safe and Resta_d on Llama3-8B 'completely destroys' the model's language ability, a severe failure mode that is not discussed or analyzed in the main text; Table 6 also shows a case (Qwen2-7B, w/ Both) where task performance drops below some baselines.

No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple-run variance is reported anywhere in the experiments, despite small evaluation sets (50–110 samples per attack type) and small absolute differences between methods in several comparisons.

ASR is computed via a rule-based keyword-matching heuristic known in the literature to be unreliable, and the GPT-4o-based harmfulness judge is used without any human validation or inter-rater agreement check.

Reproducibility is weak: the 200 manually annotated security-related instruction pairs and the search algorithm implementation are not clearly released or described in sufficient detail (e.g., exact annotation/filtering protocol for converting malicious to benign instructions), making independent replication difficult.

The method is only evaluated with LoRA fine-tuning at a fixed rank/alpha and a single learning-rate/epoch schedule; it is unclear whether findings generalize to full fine-tuning, other PEFT methods, or different hyperparameter regimes.

Presentation issues reduce clarity: dense, acronym-heavy notation, a typo in the method's own name in the abstract ('Securty-oriented'), and figures (e.g., Fig. 3, Fig. 5) with heatmaps/axes that are difficult to parse without much closer inspection, making the claimed 'patterns' hard to verify directly from the text.

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap in the literature: while most security-preserving fine-tuning defenses focus on pre-training (data curation) or post-training (parameter re-alignment) interventions, in-training methods remain underexplored; the paper's classifier-guided approach fills this gap with a concrete algorithmic contribution (SWAT).

The mechanistic analysis is thorough and internally consistent: the paper first demonstrates security feature space drift via classifier cross-testing (Table 1), then conducts a systematic module-level robustness analysis (Fig. 3) that reveals interpretable patterns (depth-dependence, module-combination effects, module-type differences), and finally builds the ModsRob search and SWAT strategy directly on these findings.

Extensive empirical validation across three LLM families (Llama2-7B, Llama3-8B, Qwen2-7B), two IFT datasets (UltraInteract, GSM8K), two training scenarios (Benign/Attack IFT), and six red-team/jailbreak evaluation protocols, with comparisons against four strong baselines (LoRAsafe, IFTsafe, Resta, Restad).

Supporting analyses (performance of the intermediate Mwarm checkpoint, parameter update magnitude comparisons, and independent verification of PATTERN A via direct early-vs-deep layer tuning) provide converging evidence for the proposed causal mechanism rather than relying solely on the main results table.
The method is shown to be complementary to existing pre-/post-training defenses, generally yielding further improvements when combined, which strengthens the practical relevance of the contribution.
Reasonable reproducibility: hyperparameters, data sources, evaluation protocols, and the ModsRob search procedure (pseudocode in the appendix) are specified in sufficient detail for replication.
weaknesses: The claim that SWAT 'can be seamlessly integrated' with other methods is contradicted by results in the appendix: combining SWAT with both IFTsafe and Restad completely destroys Llama3-8B's language ability (Table 5) and yields a negative task-performance delta for Qwen2-7B (Table 6). These failure cases are only mentioned in the appendix tables and not discussed or analyzed in the main text, which undercuts the paper's central 'greater improvement when combined' narrative.

The only directly comparable prior in-training method (Wei et al., 2024b, parameter freezing) is discussed extensively in the introduction/related work as motivation but is never included as an empirical baseline in the main experiments, making it hard to verify the claimed superiority over the closest related approach.

The ModsRob search algorithm (Alg. 1) is a hand-crafted heuristic (depth-first + breadth search) tuned to the three specific models studied; its generalizability to substantially different architectures, scales (e.g., >13B), or families beyond Llama/Qwen is untested, limiting confidence in broader applicability.

No variance/confidence intervals or multiple-seed results are reported for any experiment, so the statistical reliability of reported ASR/HS differences (some of which are small, e.g., a few percentage points) cannot be assessed; some jailbreak test sets are quite small (50 samples for PAIR/AutoDAN), amplifying this concern.

The evidence for 'security feature space drift' as the causal driver of security degradation is indirect, resting on a proxy binary classifier trained on a small, manually curated 200-pair dataset; the link between classifier accuracy changes and actual downstream security behavior, while plausible, is not independently validated beyond correlation.

Task performance is evaluated only via accuracy on the specific reasoning benchmarks used for tuning (UltraInteract/GSM8K), without broader general-capability or fluency evaluation, so potential quality degradation from the warm-up/robust-module strategy is not fully characterized (the Llama3-8B 'w Both' collapse suggests such risks exist).
